questions.q: A village once decided the dates of its harvest festival from the changing seasons and the phases of the Moon, but its elders still quarrelled over when, within one day, a 40-minute meeting should begin and end. Using the chapter's account of how timekeeping developed, (a) name the repeating natural events that gave people their calendars, and (b) explain why a calendar could not settle the meeting's timing and what people made to deal with it.
questions.a: (a) The rising and setting of the Sun (which defined the day), the phases of the Moon and the changing seasons. (b) Calendars count days, months and seasons; to measure smaller intervals within a day people made devices such as sundials, water clocks, hourglasses and candle clocks.
s: Names the Sun's rising and setting, the Moon's phases and the seasons as the repeating events
Says a calendar handles days, months and seasons, not smaller intervals within a day
Names devices made for smaller intervals, such as the sundial, water clock, hourglass or candle clock

questions.q: Sameer says, "On a day of thick cloud, the sundial, the water clock, the hourglass and the candle clock will all keep working." Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. The water clock, hourglass and candle clock do not depend on the Sun, so cloud does not stop them. A sundial reads the position of a shadow cast by sunlight, so with thick cloud it gives no reading.
s: Gives the verdict 'partly right'
Says the water clock, hourglass and candle clock do not depend on sunlight
Says the sundial needs a shadow cast by the Sun, so it fails in thick cloud

questions.q: Two identical bottle water clocks hold the same amount of water, but the cap of clock B has a bigger hole than clock A. Rohan wants to use the minute marks made for clock A on clock B. What will happen?
questions.a: A bigger hole changes how fast the water drips, so the minute marks of clock A are wrong for clock B; marks must be made again against a watch.
o: B empties sooner, so it needs new marks made with a watch
Both clocks empty together because the water quantity is the same
B shows time better because the water drips out faster
B takes longer to empty because a bigger hole is harder to fill

questions.q: Gauri has an hourglass whose sand runs from the upper bulb to the lower in exactly 4 minutes; its bulbs carry no markings. She starts it with all the sand in the upper bulb to time a 10-minute reading and turns it over the instant it runs out. (a) After two complete runs, how many minutes of the reading are still left? (b) Why can the hourglass alone not show those last minutes exactly?
questions.a: (a) Two runs are 2 x 4 = 8 minutes, so 10 - 8 = 2 minutes are left. (b) It signals only when all the sand has flowed down, a full 4 minutes; with no markings on the bulbs it cannot show a part of a run exactly.
s: Part (a): 8 minutes used, so 2 minutes left
Part (b): it signals only a complete run, with no markings to show a part of it

questions.q: Anika reads the time on a sundial in a Jaipur courtyard as 10:48 am, while her phone, which shows Indian Standard Time, reads 11:02 am. Her brother says the sundial must be faulty. What is the best conclusion?
questions.a: The chapter says a sundial measures local or solar time and needs a correction to give Indian Standard Time, so the different readings do not make the sundial faulty. A claim that two timekeepers must always agree ignores the correction; the shadow's speed is not the reason.
o: It shows local solar time, so IST needs a correction
It is faulty, since correct timekeepers must always agree
The phone is wrong, since only the Sun gives true time
The shadow is slow, so a sundial always lags by minutes

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A floating bowl with a fine hole in a water clock measures the same interval each time it sinks.
Reason (R): An hourglass measures time by the flow of sand from one bulb to another.
questions.a: Both true. R describes a different device and does not explain why the bowl gives a fixed interval (the hole sets a fixed filling time).
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Create a short situation in which a person needs a timer that works without sunlight and without electricity. Name the early device you would give her and justify the choice.
questions.a: Example: A student must time 10 minutes of silent reading in the evening during a power cut. A candle clock or hourglass works because it needs no sunlight and no electricity.
s: Gives a realistic situation without sunlight or electricity
Names a suitable device such as a candle clock, hourglass or water clock
Justifies: it does not depend on a shadow or on electricity

questions.q: Priya says, "A candle clock and an hourglass can both be used over and over for the same interval." (a) For which of the two is she wrong? (b) Say how the other one is made to measure its interval again.
questions.a: (a) The candle clock: the candle burns down as it measures, so it is used up. (b) The hourglass: its sand has only moved from one bulb to the other, so it is turned over and the sand runs back.
s: Part (a): the candle clock, because it burns away as it measures
Part (b): the hourglass is turned over so the sand flows back through the bulbs

questions.q: A hall attendant must time a 72-minute lecture. She may use the bottle water clock of Activity 8.1, which drips out in 9 minutes and is poured back after every run, or a floating-bowl clock that sinks in 24 minutes and is refloated after every sinking. Counting complete runs, how many more does the bottle clock need than the bowl clock?
questions.a: The bottle clock needs 72 / 9 = 8 runs and the bowl needs 72 / 24 = 3 runs, so 8 - 3 = 5 more. Giving 8 or 3 stops at one clock's count; 21 subtracts 3 from 24, which is not a count from this data.

questions.q: Three groups build the bottle water clock of Activity 8.1, and each makes one mistake. Group Q draws its marks 2 cm apart with a ruler and calls each gap 1 minute. Group R makes a bigger hole in the cap after marking the levels with a watch, and then uses the old marks. Group S starts a quiz when the level is already at the 2nd mark and, when the level reaches the 7th mark, announces that the quiz lasted 7 minutes. For each group (i) state the effect of the mistake, and (ii) say which of the three mistakes spoils the clock's marks for every later use and which is only a wrong reading on that occasion.
questions.a: Q: the flow slows as the level falls, so equal gaps are not equal minutes; the marks must be made again against a watch. R: water now drips faster, so the old marks are reached too soon and show more minutes than have passed; the marks must be made again. S: the quiz began at the 2nd mark, so it lasted 7 - 2 = 5 minutes, not 7. Q and R spoil the marks for every later use; S is only a reading slip on that occasion.
s: Group Q: the water level does not fall evenly because the flow slows as the level drops, so equal gaps are not equal minutes
Group R: the hole is bigger so water drips faster and the old marks are reached too soon, showing more minutes than have passed
Group S: the quiz began at the 2nd mark, so the quiz lasted 7 - 2 = 5 minutes
Says Q and R spoil the marks for every later use (new marks needed against a watch)
Says S is only a wrong reading on that occasion; the marks themselves are fine

questions.q: The bowl of a Ghatika-yantra sinks 24 minutes after it is floated. A watchman floats it at the start of his duty, dozes off, and wakes to find the bowl resting at the bottom, since no one lifted and floated it again. What can he correctly say?
questions.a: The bowl sank after 24 minutes, but nothing counted further intervals after that, so he knows only that at least 24 minutes have passed. Saying exactly 24 minutes forgets that the bowl may have sat at the bottom for a long time.
o: At least 24 minutes have passed, but how much longer is unknown
Exactly 24 minutes have passed since he floated the bowl
The bowl has measured his whole duty and the shift is over
The bowl has measured only 12 minutes, as the water level lifted it

questions.q: A school wants a timer for 40-minute evening classes held in rooms where no sunlight reaches. Compare the sundial and the candle clock for this job: (i) what each needs to work, (ii) what each can show, (iii) what happens to each over use, and (iv) decide which one the school should choose and why.
questions.a: The sundial needs sunlight to cast a shadow; the candle clock needs only to be lit. The sundial shows the time of day from the position of the shadow, while the candle clock shows the time passed since it was lit, from the burning against its markings. The candle is used up as it measures; the sundial is not. In rooms with no sunlight in the evening the sundial gives no reading, so the school should choose the candle clock.
s: States that the sundial needs sunlight and the candle clock needs only a flame
Says the sundial shows time of day from the shadow position while the candle clock shows time passed since it was lit
Says the candle is used up as it measures while the sundial is not
Concludes the candle clock suits rooms and evenings without sunlight
Gives the reason that a sundial has no shadow to read in the evening or indoors

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
Column I
1. The hole in the cap of a bottle water clock is enlarged after the marks were made
2. A sundial in a courtyard on a thickly clouded morning
3. A candle clock with 12 equal markings, burnt down to the 4th marking
4. A floating bowl found at the bottom with nobody to refloat it
Column II
a. No shadow forms, so no time can be read
b. It is known only that at least one interval has passed
c. The old marks are reached sooner than the minutes they stand for
d. One third of the burning time has passed
questions.a: Enlarged hole - water drips faster, so the old marks are reached early (c); cloudy sundial - no shadow (a); candle burnt to 4 of 12 markings - 4/12 = one third (d); sunk bowl - at least one interval known (b).

questions.q:
Statement I: A bottle water clock whose cap hole has been enlarged can still be read with its old minute marks if it is filled to the same level.
Statement II: After each sinking of a floating-bowl clock, someone must lift and float the bowl again for the clock to go on measuring.
Statement III: A candle clock shows the time that has passed since it was lit, whereas a sundial gives the time from where the shadow falls.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: II and III are correct. I is false: a bigger hole changes how fast the water drips, so the old marks no longer stand for minutes.

questions.q: The shadow on the scale of the Samrat Yantra moves about 1 mm each second and its scale shows intervals as short as 2 seconds. (a) How far does the shadow move between two marks that are 2 seconds apart? (b) A small garden sundial has a shadow that moves only 1 mm each minute. How far would its shadow move in 2 seconds, and why does that make it unsuitable for marking 2-second intervals?
questions.a: (a) 1 mm/s x 2 s = 2 mm. (b) 1 mm in 60 s means 2/60 = about 0.03 mm in 2 s, far too small a distance to mark on a scale; a large sundial spreads the shadow's movement over a long scale.
s: Part (a): 2 mm
Part (b): about 0.03 mm, too small to mark, whereas the large sundial gives a movement that a scale can mark

questions.q:
Shalini visits her grandparents in a village in Rajasthan. In the courtyard a pointed stone stands on a flat slab, and the villagers once used the moving shadow of its tip to decide the time for collecting milk. Milk must be collected at 7:00 am every day, also through the monsoon. On a rainy day last week no shadow could be seen and the milk collector came late. Shalini's cousin suggests a candle clock: a 12 cm candle marked so that 1 cm burns in 10 minutes. The family's wall clock is broken, but they have an old alarm clock that can be set to ring at any time, though its face is cracked and cannot be read.
(a) Name the device the villagers used and say what it relies on to show the time.
(b) Why could nobody read the time on the rainy day?
(c) For how long will the 12 cm candle show time once lit?
(d) Decide how the family should arrange milk collection on clear and on rainy mornings, and say how the alarm clock helps the candle clock.
questions.a: (a) Sundial; the changing position of the shadow cast by the Sun. (b) No sunlight, so no shadow. (c) 12 x 10 = 120 minutes = 2 hours. (d) Read the sundial on clear mornings. On rainy mornings set the alarm for 5:00 am, light the candle when it rings and treat the moment 12 cm has burnt, 2 hours later, as 7:00 am; the candle shows only the time since it was lit, so the alarm supplies the known starting time.
s: Part (a): sundial, relying on the shadow cast by sunlight
Part (b): no sunlight on a rainy day, so no shadow
Part (c): 12 x 10 = 120 minutes = 2 hours
Part (d): sundial on clear mornings; on rainy mornings alarm at 5:00 am to light the candle, which then ends 2 hours later at 7:00 am

questions.q: A 15 cm candle clock is marked so that 3 cm of it burns in 20 minutes. After 9 cm has burnt, ___ minutes have passed.
True or False: If the hole in the bowl of a floating-bowl water clock is made bigger, the bowl will sink in less time than before.
questions.a: True. A bigger hole lets water fill the bowl faster, so it reaches the sinking point sooner and the interval it measures becomes shorter; the interval is fixed by the hole, so the clock would need to be calibrated again.
s: Gives the verdict True
Reason: a bigger hole fills the bowl faster, so the fixed interval shortens

questions.q: Four students suggest ways to time a 30-minute test in a village hall at 8 pm, with no electricity and a cloudy sky. Whose suggestion cannot work?
questions.a: A shadow needs sunlight, and at 8 pm under cloud there is none, so Kabir's idea fails. Asha's candle (6 x 5 = 30 min), Bhumi's hourglass (10 x 3 = 30 min) and Chetan's bottle clock (5 x 6 = 30 min) do not depend on the Sun.
o: Kabir: fix a stick outdoors and read where its shadow falls
Asha: light a candle marked in cm, where 1 cm burns in 5 minutes, and stop when 6 cm have burnt
Bhumi: use a 3-minute hourglass and turn it over ten times in a row
Chetan: use a bottle clock that drips out in 6 minutes, poured back for five runs

questions.q: Compare the two types of water clock in the chapter on (a) what the observer looks at to know how much time has passed, and (b) what must be done to start the measurement again.
questions.a: (a) In the outflow type the observer reads the water level against time markings on the vessel; in the floating-bowl type the observer waits for the bowl to fill and sink. (b) The outflow vessel has to be refilled; the sunk bowl has to be lifted and floated again.
s: Part (a): level against markings versus the bowl sinking
Part (b): refill the vessel versus lift and float the bowl again

questions.q:
Ishaan's group builds a bottle water clock for the school science fair, as in Activity 8.1. They fill the upper half with coloured water and mark the level after every one minute, numbering the marks 1, 2, 3 ... from the top as the level falls. All the water takes 9 minutes to drip down, so the marks run from 1 to 9. During a relay race at the fair, an observer sees the level touch the 5th mark when the race starts and the 8th mark when it ends. Later the teacher wants to time a 20-minute written test using this clock.
(a) Which instrument did the group need to make the marks, and why?
(b) How long did the relay race last?
(c) A second race lasts 4 minutes 30 seconds. Can this clock show that time exactly? Explain.
(d) Decide how the 9-minute clock can be used to time the 20-minute test.
questions.a: (a) A watch, so the marks stand for exact minutes. (b) 3 min. (c) No; only whole-minute marks exist, so 4 min 30 s lies halfway between two marks. (d) Run it twice for 18 min and then to the 2nd mark: 9 + 9 + 2 = 20 min.
s: Part (a): a watch, to know when each minute has passed
Part (b): 8 - 5 = 3 minutes
Part (c): no; marks are made only for whole minutes, so 4 min 30 s falls between the 4th and 5th marks
Part (d): use it twice (18 minutes) and a third time up to the 2-minute mark, 9 + 9 + 2 = 20

questions.q:
A temple town keeps a Ghatika-yantra running day and night: its bowl sinks every 24 minutes, and the attendant on duty refloats it and strikes the gong each time. The trust can choose between Plan P, three attendants on 8-hour shifts paid ₹400 per shift, and Plan Q, two attendants on 12-hour shifts paid ₹550 per shift. Once, a tired attendant on a long shift dozed off and the gongs for the sinkings he missed were never struck.
(a) How many gongs does one attendant strike in an 8-hour shift and in a 12-hour shift?
(b) What is the daily wage bill under each plan?
(c) How much does Plan Q save in a year of 365 days?
(d) Decide between the plans and justify your choice using (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) 20 gongs in 8 hours and 30 gongs in 12 hours. (b) Plan P: ₹1,200; Plan Q: ₹1,100. (c) ₹100 a day, so ₹36,500 a year. (d) Either plan is acceptable if the reasoning uses the numbers. For example, Plan P is chosen because the bowl's whole purpose is equal, unbroken intervals, and a shorter shift of 20 sinkings lowers the chance of a lapse, at a cost of ₹36,500 a year; Plan Q is chosen if the saving of ₹36,500 matters more and the longer 30-sinking shifts are managed.
s: Part (d): a decision backed by the shift length of 20 or 30 sinkings and the saving of ₹36,500

questions.q: Galileo (1564-1642) studied swinging pendulums and found that a pendulum of a given length takes the same time for each oscillation. Christiaan Huygens (1629-1695) invented the pendulum clock in 1656. (a) How old was Huygens when Galileo died? (b) How many years after Galileo's death was the pendulum clock invented? (c) For how many years after the invention did Huygens live? (d) Explain why Galileo's finding, and not just the fact that a pendulum swings, is what a clock needs.
questions.a: (a) 1642 - 1629 = 13 years. (b) 1656 - 1642 = 14 years. (c) 1695 - 1656 = 39 years. (d) A clock must mark equal intervals; because a pendulum of a given length takes the same time for each oscillation, each swing is one equal interval that can be counted, which a swing of changing duration could not give.
s: Part (a): 13 years
Part (b): 14 years
Part (c): 39 years
Part (d): a clock needs equal intervals to count
Part (d): same time for each oscillation of a given length gives equal intervals

questions.q: A potter copies the bowl of a Ghatika-yantra but makes the fine hole wider. (a) Will his bowl sink in more than, less than or exactly 24 minutes, and why? (b) What does this do to the number of sinkings in one day?
questions.a: (a) Less than 24 minutes: a wider hole lets the bowl fill sooner, and the hole is what fixes the interval. (b) The sinkings in a day become more than 60, so the day no longer divides into 60 equal ghatis of 24 minutes.
s: Part (a): less than 24 minutes because the wider hole fills the bowl sooner
Part (b): more than 60 sinkings in a day, so the ghati of 24 minutes is no longer the unit

questions.q: In an outflow water clock the water level fell by 8 cm in the first hour, 6 cm in the second hour and 4.5 cm in the third hour. A student marks the vessel every 8 cm and labels each gap '1 hour', because the first hour took the level 8 cm down. (a) Does the level fall by equal amounts in equal times? (b) What time will her scale read after 2 real hours? (c) By how many minutes does it under-read at that moment? (d) Give the chapter's reason for the pattern. (e) Say why a bowl that sinks after a fixed time does not have this problem.
questions.a: (a) No: 8, 6 and 4.5 cm are unequal. (b) The level has fallen 8 + 6 = 14 cm, so the scale reads 14 / 8 = 1.75 hours. (c) 2 - 1.75 = 0.25 h = 15 minutes. (d) The flow rate decreases as the water level drops. (e) The bowl fills and sinks in the same fixed time every time, so every interval is equal whatever the water level.
s: Part (a): unequal falls, so no
Part (b): 14 cm gives a reading of 1.75 hours
Part (c): 0.25 h = 15 minutes
Part (d): flow rate decreases as the water level drops
Part (e): the bowl's fill-and-sink time is fixed by its hole, not by the water level

questions.q: A priest says a temple ritual lasted 7.5 ghatis, the unit the Ghatika-yantra gave. How long did the ritual last?
questions.a: One ghati is the 24 minutes the bowl took to fill and sink, so 7.5 x 24 = 180 minutes = 3 hours. Reading a ghati as an hour gives 7 hours 30 minutes; dropping the half ghati gives 7 x 24 = 168 minutes = 2 hours 48 minutes.

questions.q: Galileo's pulse beat 72 times a minute. In church he counted 15 beats while a hanging lamp made 5 complete swings, and the lamp took the same time for each swing. What was the time for one swing?
questions.a: 15 beats at 72 beats a minute take 15 / 72 x 60 = 12.5 s for 5 swings, so one swing takes 12.5 / 5 = 2.5 s. Giving 3 takes beats for seconds; 12.5 s is the time for all 5 swings; 0.4 inverts the working.

questions.q: The attendant of a Ghatika-yantra, whose bowl always sinks 24 minutes after it is floated, struck the 10th gong 4 hours 30 minutes after sunrise. The hole has not changed. What does this show?
questions.a: Ten sinkings of 24 minutes take 240 minutes = 4 hours, but 4 hours 30 minutes passed, so 30 minutes were lost because the bowl waited between sinking and refloating. The hole is unchanged, so the sinking time stays 24 minutes.
o: Refloating was delayed by 30 minutes in all
The bowl sank ten times in exactly the expected time
Each sinking now takes 27 minutes, since the hole has become smaller
The attendant struck three extra gongs before the 10th

questions.q: Rahul says, "The Ghatika-yantra became useless the day the pendulum clock was invented in 1656." Check his claim using the chapter.
questions.a: No. The pendulum clock was invented in the seventeenth century, but the Ghatika-yantra was only progressively replaced by pendulum clocks in the late nineteenth century, more than two centuries later, and it continued to be used at religious places for rituals.
s: Gives the verdict No
Says it was replaced progressively only in the late nineteenth century, about two centuries after 1656
Says it still continued at religious places for rituals

questions.q: The Arthasastra, composed and revised between the second century BCE and the third century CE, has the earliest reference to shadow-based timekeeping in the chapter; Varahamihira gave an accurate expression for time from the shadow of a vertical stick around 530 CE; Huygens invented the pendulum clock in 1656. (a) How many years after Varahamihira's expression was the pendulum clock invented? (b) Is Varahamihira's expression older or newer than the end of the Arthasastra period? Give the reason. (c) Which is the older source of shadow-based timekeeping?
questions.a: (a) 1656 - 530 = 1126 years. (b) Newer, because 530 CE lies in the sixth century CE, after the third century CE in which the Arthasastra period ends. (c) The Arthasastra reference.
s: Part (a): 1126 years
Part (b): newer, since 530 CE is in the sixth century, after the third century CE
Part (c): the Arthasastra reference is older

questions.q: A student says a Ghatika-yantra could announce 70 ghatis in one 24-hour day. Show with numbers that this is impossible.
questions.a: A day holds 1440 / 24 = 60 ghatis. 70 ghatis would need 70 x 24 = 1680 min = 28 h, more than a day.
s: Day = 24 x 60 = 1440 minutes so 1440 / 24 = 60 ghatis
70 x 24 = 1680 minutes
1680 minutes is 28 hours, more than the 24-hour day

questions.q:
Students from a Jaipur school visit the Samrat Yantra. The guide says it is about 300 years old, 27 metres high, and that its shadow moves at about 1 millimetre per second on a finely marked scale. A student notes that during the guide's talk the shadow edge moved 12 centimetres. Another student compares the reading with her phone, which shows Indian Standard Time, and sees a difference. The principal proposes that on sunny days a sundial like this should ring the 8:00 am assembly bell, with the wall clock used on cloudy days.
(a) How long was the guide's talk?
(b) How far will the shadow move in 15 minutes?
(c) Why does the reading differ from the phone?
(d) Do you support the principal's plan? Say what must be done to the sundial reading and what happens on a cloudy morning.
questions.a: (a) 120 s = 2 min. (b) 900 mm = 90 cm. (c) Local solar time differs from IST. (d) Support it with conditions: apply the correction to get IST, and keep the wall clock for cloudy mornings when there is no shadow.
s: Part (a): 12 cm = 120 mm, at 1 mm per second = 120 s = 2 minutes
Part (c): a sundial shows local solar time, not IST
Part (d): supports only with a correction applied to get IST; on a cloudy morning no shadow forms, so the wall clock is needed

questions.q: True or False: Varahamihira's accurate expression for time from the shadow of a vertical stick, around 530 CE, is older than the Arthasastra's reference to shadow-based timekeeping.
questions.a: False. The Arthasastra, composed and revised between the second century BCE and the third century CE, has the earliest reference to shadow-based timekeeping; 530 CE falls after that period.
s: Gives the verdict False
Reason: the Arthasastra period ended in the third century CE, before 530 CE

questions.q: Early pendulum clocks could gain or lose 10 seconds each day. A clock gains 10 seconds every day. (a) After how many days will it be a full minute ahead? (b) How many minutes ahead will it be after 90 days?
questions.a: (a) 60 s / 10 s a day = 6 days. (b) 90 x 10 = 900 s = 15 minutes.
s: Part (a): 6 days
Part (b): 900 s = 15 minutes

questions.q:
Statement I: In outflow water clocks the flow rate decreased as the water level dropped, which made their markings unreliable.
Statement II: A Ghatika-yantra whose bowl sinks every 24 minutes and is refloated at once strikes the gong 36 times in 12 hours.
Statement III: Huygens invented the pendulum clock 14 years after Galileo died.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: I and III are correct. II is false: 12 hours is 720 minutes and 720 / 24 = 30 gongs, not 36. III is true: 1656 - 1642 = 14.

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
Column I
1. The flow from an outflow water clock slowed as its level fell
2. Galileo found that a pendulum of a given length takes the same time for each swing
3. People began to travel long distances
4. The hole of the bowl was made so that it took 24 minutes to fill and sink
Column II
a. A day was divided into 60 equal ghatis
b. The sinking-bowl clock was developed
c. Increasingly better mechanical devices for time were developed
d. Huygens was inspired to make a pendulum clock
questions.a: Slowing flow of the outflow clock - the sinking bowl was developed (b); Galileo's finding - inspired Huygens (d); long-distance travel - better mechanical devices (c); 24-minute bowl - a day of 60 ghatis (a).

questions.q: A visitor to the Samrat Yantra at Jantar Mantar is told that it is about 27 metres high, its shadow moves about 1 millimetre per second, and its scale is finely marked to measure intervals as short as 2 seconds. Which conclusion is NOT supported?
questions.a: The shortest interval its scale can measure is 2 seconds, so it cannot resolve two events that are 1 second apart.
o: It can separate two events that happen 1 second apart
Its shadow moves 2 mm during the shortest interval it measures
Its reading is local solar time and needs a correction for IST
It is a sundial, so it cannot work in the dark

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In an outflow water clock, equal falls of the water level take equal times.
Reason (R): The flow rate of an outflow water clock decreases as the water level drops.
questions.a: A is false and R is true. Because the flow slows as the level drops, the level falls by less in each later hour, so equal falls take unequal times.
o: A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: An attendant strikes the 3rd gong of a Ghatika-yantra at 7:12 am and the 19th gong later the same day, refloating the bowl promptly each time. (a) How long is it from the 3rd to the 19th gong? (b) At what time is the 19th gong struck?
questions.a: (a) There are 19 - 3 = 16 sinkings in between, and 16 x 24 = 384 minutes = 6 hours 24 minutes. (b) 7:12 am + 6 h 24 min = 1:36 pm.
s: Part (a): 16 intervals x 24 minutes = 6 hours 24 minutes
Part (b): 1:36 pm

questions.q: Create two short situations. In the first a sinking-bowl clock helps but a sundial cannot. In the second the sinking-bowl clock gives a wrong time but a sundial still works. Give the reason in each.
questions.a: First: a night-time ritual in a monastery, where there is no sunlight and no shadow, but the bowl keeps measuring equal intervals. Second: on a sunny day the attendant falls asleep and does not refloat the bowl after it sinks; the intervals are no longer counted, but the sundial shows the time from the shadow without anyone's help.
s: First situation at night or in cloud, with the reason that no shadow forms
Second situation in which the bowl is not refloated or counted, with the reason that its intervals are lost
Says the sundial still works on a sunny day without anyone's help

questions.q: A craftsman makes a bowl clock that sinks every 18 minutes. A day has 1440 minutes, so the day holds ___ such sinkings.

A guide at Jantar Mantar says the Samrat Yantra was built about 300 years before 2025. (a) In about which year was it built? (b) Was it built before or after Huygens' pendulum clock of 1656, and by about how many years?
questions.a: (a) 2025 - 300 = 1725. (b) After, by about 1725 - 1656 = 69, so roughly 70 years.
s: Part (a): about 1725
Part (b): after, by about 70 years

questions.q: Ravi's simple pendulum has a time period of 1.8 s. He releases the bob from the extreme position A and stops the stopwatch when the bob is back at A for the 7th time (the release itself is not counted). What does the stopwatch read?
questions.a: Each return to A is one complete oscillation of 1.8 s, so 7 returns take 7 x 1.8 = 12.6 s. Counting the release as the first return gives 6 x 1.8 = 10.8 s; 14.4 s counts 8 oscillations; 3.89 s divides 7 by 1.8.

questions.q: For Activity 8.2 Meera has a 150 cm string. She ties the bob at one end and winds 30 cm of the other end around the rigid support so that the rest hangs down to the bob. What length should she write in her Table 8.1?
questions.a: The length of a simple pendulum is the length of string hanging between the support and the bob, which is 150 - 30 = 120 cm. The whole string length of 150 cm includes the part wound round the support; 30 cm is only the wound part.

questions.q:
Pooja must set up a lab pendulum that completes one oscillation every 2 seconds (30 oscillations in a minute). In the store room she finds a 100 cm thread, a 150 cm thread, a 50 g bob and a 200 g bob. The 100 cm thread is frayed and can safely carry only the 50 g bob; the 150 cm thread can carry either bob, but she may not cut, wind or knot any thread. She times 10 oscillations for three set-ups, treating each as a simple pendulum. Set-up 1: 100 cm thread, 50 g bob, 20.0 s. Set-up 2: 150 cm thread, 50 g bob, 24.6 s. Set-up 3: 150 cm thread, 200 g bob, 24.8 s.
(a) Find the time period of each set-up.
(b) What do set-ups 2 and 3 show about the bob's mass?
(c) What do set-ups 1 and 2 show about the length?
(d) Which thread and bob should Pooja use, and why can she not simply pick the strongest pair?
questions.a: (a) 2.00 s, 2.46 s, 2.48 s. (b) Mass does not change the period: the same 150 cm thread gives almost equal periods with 50 g and 200 g. (c) The longer thread gives the longer period. (d) The 100 cm thread with the 50 g bob: it gives 2.00 s, and the stronger 150 cm thread cannot be shortened, so with either bob it gives about 2.5 s, not 2 s.
s: Part (a): 2.00 s, 2.46 s and 2.48 s
Part (b): equal length, different mass, almost equal period, so mass does not matter
Part (c): the 150 cm thread gives a longer period than the 100 cm thread
Part (d): 100 cm thread with the 50 g bob, because only the length decides the period and 150 cm gives about 2.5 s

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A student who changes the thread of a pendulum from 100 cm to 150 cm, keeping the same bob, can find that the time for 10 oscillations changes.
Reason (R): The time period of a simple pendulum depends on its length.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: because the period depends on the length, a changed length can change the time for 10 oscillations even though the bob is the same.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: A pendulum, released from the extreme position A, completes 18 oscillations in 45 s. (a) Find its time period. (b) The student keeps timing for 2 minutes. Where is the bob at the end, and how do you know?
questions.a: (a) 45 s / 18 = 2.5 s. (b) 120 s / 2.5 s = 48 complete oscillations, a whole number, so the bob is back at the extreme position A from which it was released.
s: Part (b): 48 complete oscillations, so the bob is back at A

questions.q: Three timings of 10 oscillations of the same 100 cm pendulum are taken in four groups. Which group's three readings should make the teacher suspect a mistake and ask for the activity to be repeated?
questions.a: For a pendulum of fixed length the time period is almost the same every time, so small differences are normal, but 36.1 s is far from 24 s and points to a mistake such as a miscount or a changed length. The other three sets differ by only a few tenths of a second.

questions.q: Three students record the time for 10 oscillations. A: 64 cm thread, 100 g bob, 16.1 s. B: 64 cm thread, 250 g bob, 16.0 s. C: 121 cm thread, 100 g bob, 22.0 s. (a) Find each time period. (b) Compare A and B: does mass matter? (c) Compare A and C: what does length do? (d) A says, "B's reading is 0.1 s smaller, so heavier bobs swing faster." Is she right? (e) What would you change to make a pendulum's time period longer?
questions.a: (a) 1.61 s, 1.60 s, 2.20 s. (b) Almost equal, so mass does not matter. (c) Longer thread, longer period. (d) No; the 0.1 s is ordinary variation at the same length. (e) Lengthen the thread.
s: Part (a): 1.61 s, 1.60 s and 2.20 s
Part (b): the periods are almost equal, so mass does not matter
Part (c): the longer thread has the longer time period
Part (d): not right; the small difference is the usual variation, since length is the same
Part (e): lengthen the thread

questions.q: Nikhil counts every movement of the bob from one extreme position to the other as one oscillation. For 10 'oscillations' by his count the stopwatch shows 12.5 s, and he writes a time period of 1.25 s. What is the true time period?
questions.a: His 10 counts are one-way movements, A to B and B to A, so they make only 5 complete oscillations; the true time period is 12.5 / 5 = 2.5 s. His 1.25 s halves the real value; 5.0 s multiplies it wrongly; 0.8 s is the inverse of 1.25.

questions.q: Aman times his pendulum for 10 oscillations and gets 23 s. He writes: "The time period of my pendulum is 23 s." (a) Find his mistake. (b) Give the correct time period.
questions.a: (a) 23 s is the time for 10 oscillations; the time period is the time for one oscillation. (b) 23 s / 10 = 2.3 s.
s: (a) He gave the time for 10 oscillations as the time period of one oscillation

questions.q: True or False: A pendulum bob that starts from its mean position O, goes to the extreme position A and comes straight back to O has completed one oscillation.
questions.a: False. One oscillation needs O to A, then on to the other extreme B, then back to O (or A to B and back to A). Going from O to A and back to O is only half of it.
s: Verdict: False
Reason or correction that rests on the chapter

questions.q: A student claims that the same pendulum took 20 s for 10 oscillations and also 40 s for 25 oscillations, both at the same place. Show that both readings cannot be true.
questions.a: 2 s versus 1.6 s. The time period of a pendulum of a given length is constant at a place, so the readings contradict each other.
s: Time period from first reading = 20 / 10 = 2 s
Time period from second reading = 40 / 25 = 1.6 s
A pendulum of given length has one constant time period, so 2 s and 1.6 s cannot both hold

questions.q: Asha times 10 oscillations of a 100 cm pendulum and gets 20.0 s. Ravi times 30 oscillations of the same pendulum and gets 60.3 s. Ravi says, "Our time periods must be almost the same even though our times are so different." Do you agree?
questions.a: Yes. Asha's time period is 20.0 / 10 = 2.00 s and Ravi's is 60.3 / 30 = 2.01 s. The time period of a pendulum of a given length is constant at a place, so a longer timing gives a longer total but the same time for one oscillation.
s: Gives the verdict that he is right
Works out 2.00 s and 2.01 s
Reason: the time period of a pendulum of a given length is constant at a place

questions.q:
At a mela a swing has chains of equal length; treat the swing as a simple pendulum. The operator times Ananya's ride and finds that she completes 12 oscillations in 30 seconds. Her younger brother Veer, who is lighter, then takes the same swing. The swing is available for 2 hours (120 minutes) and 40 children are waiting. Changing riders takes 30 seconds. The operator can offer either a ride of 3 minutes or a ride of 60 oscillations.
(a) Find the time period of Ananya's swing.
(b) How many oscillations are there in a 3-minute ride?
(c) What happens to the time period when lighter Veer rides? Why?
(d) Which ride option lets all 40 children ride, and why?
questions.a: (a) 2.5 s. (b) 72. (c) It stays almost the same; mass does not matter. (d) The 60-oscillation ride: 150 s + 30 s = 3 min per child, 120 min in all. The 3-minute ride needs 3.5 min per child, 140 min, which does not fit.
s: Part (b): 180 / 2.5 = 72 oscillations
Part (c): almost unchanged, since mass does not affect the time period
Part (d): 60 oscillations = 150 s, plus 30 s changing = 3 min a child, 40 x 3 = 120 min fits; the 3-minute ride needs 40 x 3.5 = 140 min

questions.q: Anil times 10 oscillations of his pendulum and gets 25.5 s. Sita hangs a bob of three times the mass on a thread of the same length and times 20 oscillations. Her stopwatch should read about ___ s.
Meena wants evidence that the mass of the bob does not affect the time period. Which pair of readings for 10 oscillations is the best evidence?
questions.a: The test changes only the mass and keeps the thread length the same: 100 cm with 50 g and with 200 g both give almost the same time. The other pairs change the length too, so they cannot isolate the mass.
o: 100 cm thread: 50 g bob 20.0 s and 200 g bob 20.1 s
100 cm thread with 50 g bob 20.0 s; 150 cm thread with 200 g bob 24.6 s
100 cm thread with 50 g bob 20.0 s; 150 cm thread with 50 g bob 24.6 s
64 cm thread with 100 g bob 16.1 s; 121 cm thread with 250 g bob 22.0 s

questions.q: Four groups time 10 oscillations of simple pendulums that all have a 100 cm thread. Group 1 gets 20.2 s, Group 2 gets 19.8 s, Group 3 gets 20.0 s and Group 4 gets 26.0 s. Group 4 says its bob was the heaviest. (a) Find the mean time for 10 oscillations of Groups 1 to 3 and their time period. (b) Find Group 4's time period. (c) By how much does it differ from that of the other groups? (d) Can the heavier bob explain the difference? (e) Name one thing Group 4 should check.
questions.a: (a) The mean is (20.2 + 19.8 + 20.0) / 3 = 20.0 s, so the time period is 2.0 s. (b) 26.0 / 10 = 2.6 s. (c) 2.6 - 2.0 = 0.6 s. (d) No; the time period does not depend on the mass of the bob. (e) The length of its thread between the support and the bob (or whether it counted the oscillations correctly).
s: Part (a): mean 20.0 s and time period 2.0 s
Part (b): 2.6 s
Part (c): 0.6 s
Part (d): mass does not change the time period, so the heavy bob is not the cause
Part (e): check the length of the thread or the counting of oscillations

questions.q:
Statement I: The time period of a pendulum is found by dividing the time for a number of oscillations by that number.
Statement II: The motion of a pendulum is periodic because the bob repeats its path after a fixed interval of time.
Statement III: To start the oscillations properly, the bob should be given a gentle push at the moment it is released.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: I and II are correct. III is false: the bob should be moved slightly to one side and released without pushing it, with the string taut.

questions.q: In three trials of Activity 8.2 the time for 10 oscillations is 24.6 s, 24.4 s and 24.8 s. (a) Find the time period from these trials. (b) Why is the activity repeated 3 to 4 times instead of relying on one reading?
questions.a: (a) The mean time for 10 oscillations is (24.6 + 24.4 + 24.8) / 3 = 24.6 s, so the time period is 2.46 s. (b) The readings are only almost the same each time, so the mean of several trials is more dependable than a single reading.
s: Part (a): mean 24.6 s, time period 2.46 s
Part (b): readings differ slightly, so several trials are averaged

questions.q: A table for the same bob gives the time period for thread lengths: 25 cm, 1.00 s; 50 cm, 1.42 s; 100 cm, 2.01 s; 150 cm, 2.46 s. (a) A student wants 40 oscillations in 80.4 s. Which length should she choose? (b) Does doubling the length from 50 cm to 100 cm double the time period? Use the table.
questions.a: (a) 80.4 / 40 = 2.01 s, which belongs to the 100 cm thread. (b) No: the period goes from 1.42 s to 2.01 s, only about 1.4 times, not 2 times.
s: Part (a): period 2.01 s, so 100 cm
Part (b): 1.42 s to 2.01 s is about 1.4 times, not double

questions.q: Write a short experiment record (the length of the thread, the number of oscillations and the time taken) for which the time period works out to 2.5 s. Show the working. Then say what you expect the time for the same number of oscillations to be if the bob is replaced by a heavier one on the same thread.
questions.a: Example: a 150 cm thread, 10 oscillations in 25 s. Time period = 25 / 10 = 2.5 s. With a heavier bob on the same thread the time stays almost the same, about 25 s, since the time period depends on length and not on mass.
s: A record with consistent numbers, such as 10 oscillations in 25 s
Working: 25 / 10 = 2.5 s
Heavier bob, same thread: almost the same time, since mass does not matter

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Atomic clocks are more precise than Huygens' early pendulum clocks.
Reason (R): Atomic clocks work by the vibrations of a quartz crystal.
questions.a: A is true: atomic clocks lose one second in millions of years, early pendulum clocks gained or lost 10 s a day. R is false: atomic clocks use specific atoms; the quartz crystal belongs to quartz clocks.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q: A phone's processor handles one signal step in 3 microseconds, while a sports timer records an interval of 3 milliseconds. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: A microsecond is one-millionth of a second and a millisecond is one-thousandth of a second, so 3 microseconds is 3/1000 of 3 milliseconds, one-thousandth as long. Treating the two prefixes as equal, or reversing them, ignores the factor of 1000.
o: The processor's step is 1000 times shorter than the timer's interval
The processor's step is 1000 times longer than the timer's interval
The two intervals are equal since both are written as 3
The processor's step is 3 times shorter than the timer's interval

questions.q: Two sprinters are timed at 12.411 s and 12.414 s. A school timer that shows hundredths of a second displays 12.41 s for both. What is the best conclusion?
questions.a: The gap is 12.414 - 12.411 = 0.003 s = 3 ms, smaller than the 10 ms step of a hundredths timer, so both show 12.41 s; a timer reading thousandths is needed. A tenths timer or a 1 s wall clock is coarser and cannot do better.
o: Their gap is 3 milliseconds, visible only to a thousandths timer
They crossed the line at the same instant, since the timer shows equal times
A timer showing tenths of a second would separate them better
A wall clock with a 1 s division would separate them as long as it is large

questions.q: True or False: In the line 'Break: 15 min. followed by the next paper', the unit symbol is written correctly because a symbol for a unit should always end with a full stop.
questions.a: False. A full stop is not written after the symbol for a unit except at the end of a sentence; here 'min' is in the middle of the line, so it should be written '15 min' with a space after 15 and no full stop.
s: Gives the verdict False
Reason: no full stop after a unit symbol except at the end of a sentence; the correct form is 15 min

questions.q: A pendulum clock counts one swing in about 2 seconds, while a quartz clock counts the vibrations of a crystal that repeat thousands of times in a second. Which conclusion follows from the chapter?
questions.a: Modern clocks use the same basic principle of a repeating process, but with tiny and very rapid vibrations, so each repeat is a tiny interval and the clock can measure very short intervals precisely. Sharing the principle does not mean sharing the size of the interval.
o: The quartz clock marks far shorter intervals; each vibration is a tiny fraction of a second
The pendulum clock is more precise, since a single slow swing is easy to count
Both clocks mark intervals of the same size, since both rely on repeating motion
The quartz clock needs the changing shadow of an object to mark its intervals

questions.q: A stopwatch shows 5400 s for a long relay event. Which line converts it and writes it correctly using the chapter's rules for unit symbols?
questions.a: 5400 s / 3600 = 1.5 h = 1 h 30 min, written with lowercase, singular symbols and a space after each number. Writing hrs, mins or capital Hr and Min breaks the rules.

questions.q: A stopwatch shows 7523 s at the end of a trek. (a) Express this as hours, minutes and seconds. (b) Write it with the correct unit symbols, following the chapter's rules.
questions.a: (a) 7523 s = 2 x 3600 + 5 x 60 + 23, which is 2 hours 5 minutes 23 seconds. (b) 2 h 5 min 23 s, with lowercase singular symbols, a space after each number and no full stops.
s: Part (a): 2 hours 5 minutes 23 seconds
Part (b): 2 h 5 min 23 s, written with the rules for symbols

questions.q: A school has four timers: A, a wall clock whose smallest division is 1 s; B, a stopwatch showing hundredths of a second; C, a timer showing thousandths of a second; D, a chip timer working in microseconds. For each task, name the coarsest timer that can still do the job and give the reason: (i) deciding between two runners who finish 0.03 s apart; (ii) spotting heartbeat gaps that differ by 4 milliseconds; (iii) ringing the school bell at 9:00 am; (iv) timing steps of 5 microseconds in a phone; (v) timing a 50-minute examination.
questions.a: (i) B: its step of 0.01 s is smaller than 0.03 s, while A cannot show it. (ii) C: a 4 millisecond difference needs thousandths, as B's 10 millisecond step is too coarse. (iii) A: a 1 s step is more than enough for a bell. (iv) D: only microsecond timing can resolve 5 microseconds. (v) A: a 1 s step is more than enough over 50 minutes.
s: Task (i): B, because 0.01 s is less than 0.03 s
Task (ii): C, because 4 ms is below B's 10 ms step
Task (iii): A is enough for a bell
Task (iv): D, microsecond timing
Task (v): A is enough for 50 minutes

questions.q: A digital recorder captures sound by taking 8000 readings every second, evenly spaced. (a) How long is the gap between two readings, in milliseconds? (b) Express the same gap in microseconds.
questions.a: (a) 1/8000 s = 0.000125 s = 0.125 milliseconds. (b) 0.125 ms x 1000 = 125 microseconds.
s: Part (a): 0.125 milliseconds
Part (b): 125 microseconds

questions.q:
At the state athletics meet the girls' 100 m final is timed electronically to one-thousandth of a second: the winner took 12.482 s and the runner-up 12.487 s. The school wants one timer for its house races, where past gaps between the first two runners were as small as 0.03 s. The options are Timer A showing whole seconds (₹400), Timer B showing hundredths of a second (₹1,500) and Timer C showing thousandths of a second (₹6,000).
(a) Find the gap at the state meet in milliseconds.
(b) Express the school's smallest past gap, 0.03 s, in milliseconds.
(c) How many hundredths of a second is that gap, and which timers can separate the two runners?
(d) Which timer should the school buy, and why?
questions.a: (a) 5 milliseconds. (b) 30 milliseconds. (c) 3 hundredths of a second; B and C can separate them, A cannot. (d) Timer B: hundredths are enough for a 0.03 s gap and it costs ₹4,500 less than C.
s: Part (a): 12.487 - 12.482 = 0.005 s = 5 milliseconds
Part (b): 0.03 x 1000 = 30 milliseconds
Part (c): 3 hundredths; Timers B and C can separate them, Timer A cannot
Part (d): Timer B; it separates a 0.03 s gap at a lower cost than Timer C

questions.q: Imran says, "A timer that shows milliseconds measures intervals a thousand times longer than a timer that shows seconds, because 'milli' means thousand." Check his claim.
questions.a: No. A millisecond is one-thousandth of a second, so a millisecond timer can separate intervals a thousand times shorter, not longer; that is why sports timers use it to decide close finishes.
s: Gives the verdict No
States that a millisecond is one-thousandth of a second
Concludes the timer measures much shorter intervals, which suits close finishes

questions.q:
A hospital corridor has an old pendulum clock that shows only whole seconds and gains 10 s each day, like Huygens' early clocks; it is reset every morning. The ECG machine has a quartz-based timer that reads to the millisecond. For one patient the ECG records two heartbeat gaps of 0.75 s and 0.80 s. The drug chart needs times right to the nearest minute, while the ECG analysis must tell apart gaps that differ by a few tens of milliseconds. A nurse can read only one clock for each job.
(a) Express 0.75 s in milliseconds.
(b) By how much can the corridor clock be wrong at the end of a day?
(c) By how many milliseconds do the two heartbeat gaps differ?
(d) Which clock should be used for the drug chart and which for the ECG analysis? Justify with (a) to (c).
questions.a: (a) 750 milliseconds. (b) 10 seconds. (c) 50 milliseconds. (d) Use the corridor clock for the drug chart: an error of at most 10 s is far below the 1 minute needed. Use the quartz timer for the ECG: the corridor clock shows only whole seconds, so it cannot separate gaps that differ by 50 milliseconds.
s: Part (a): 750 milliseconds
Part (b): at most 10 seconds
Part (c): 50 milliseconds
Part (d): corridor clock for the drug chart (10 s error is under a minute) and quartz timer for the ECG (50 ms cannot be shown in whole seconds)

questions.q: A phone processes a signal in microseconds, one-millionth of a second, while a sports timer records milliseconds, one-thousandth of a second. (a) How many microseconds make 1 millisecond? (b) How many microseconds are there in 0.002 s?
questions.a: (a) 1000 microseconds. (b) 0.002 s is 2 milliseconds, which is 2 x 1000 = 2000 microseconds.
s: (a) 1 millisecond = 1000 microseconds, from one-thousandth against one-millionth
(b) 0.002 s = 2 ms = 2000 microseconds

questions.q: A phone's processor finishes one operation every 5 microseconds. In 1 millisecond it can finish ___ operations.
A stopwatch app shows a runner's time as 90.5 s. Which student gives a value that is correct and follows the chapter's rules for writing units of time?
questions.a: 90.5 s = 60 s + 30.5 s = 1 min 30.5 s, written with lowercase symbols and spaces. 1.5 min is only 90 s, so it loses the 0.5 s; 1 min 5 s is a wrong value; 'sec' is not a correct symbol for second.

questions.q: In a relay, Team 1's four runners take 12.45 s, 12.31 s, 12.60 s and 12.36 s. Team 2's runners take 12.40 s, 12.52 s, 12.44 s and 12.38 s. (a) Find each team's total time. (b) Find the gap between the teams in milliseconds. (c) What would a timer showing only whole seconds, and a timer showing only tenths of a second, display for each total? (d) What is the coarsest of whole seconds, tenths, hundredths and thousandths that separates the teams? (e) Write the winning team's time with the correct symbol.
questions.a: (a) Team 1: 49.72 s; Team 2: 49.74 s. (b) 0.02 s = 20 milliseconds. (c) Whole seconds: 50 s for both; tenths: 49.7 s for both. (d) Hundredths of a second, since its step of 0.01 s is less than 0.02 s. (e) Team 1 wins with 49.72 s.
s: Part (a): 49.72 s and 49.74 s
Part (b): 20 milliseconds
Part (c): both 50 s on a whole-second timer and both 49.7 s on a tenths timer
Part (d): hundredths of a second
Part (e): 49.72 s for Team 1

questions.q:
Statement I: The SI unit of time is the second, with symbol s.
Statement II: 'sec' and 'hrs' are correct symbols for second and hour.
Statement III: Quartz clocks work by vibrations of specific atoms.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Only I is correct. II is false: 'sec' and 'hrs' are incorrect. III is false: quartz clocks use a quartz crystal; atomic clocks use atoms.

questions.q: An ECG shows three successive heartbeat gaps of 0.78 s, 0.80 s and 0.76 s. (a) Write the three gaps in milliseconds. (b) What is the largest difference between two of them, in milliseconds? (c) Would a timer that shows only tenths of a second notice this variation? Explain.
questions.a: (a) 780 ms, 800 ms and 760 ms. (b) 800 - 760 = 40 ms. (c) No; to the nearest tenth of a second all three gaps would read 0.8 s, so the variation would be hidden.
s: Part (a): 780 ms, 800 ms, 760 ms
Part (b): 40 ms
Part (c): a tenths timer shows 0.8 s for all three, hiding the variation

questions.q: A student says a stopwatch that can show only tenths of a second recorded the winner's time as 12.34 s. Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: A timer that shows tenths gives one digit after the decimal point, such as 12.3 s or 12.4 s. A reading of 12.34 s needs a step of one-hundredth of a second, which this timer cannot show.
s: States that a tenths timer shows only one digit after the decimal point
Says 12.34 s needs hundredths of a second
Concludes the reading could not come from this timer

questions.q: A quartz crystal in a watch vibrates 32,768 times each second. (a) How many vibrations occur in 1 minute? (b) For how many microseconds does one vibration last, to the nearest tenth of a microsecond?
questions.a: (a) 32,768 x 60 = 1,966,080 vibrations. (b) 1 / 32,768 s = about 0.0000305 s = about 30.5 microseconds.
s: Part (a): 1,966,080 vibrations
Part (b): about 30.5 microseconds

questions.q: A train leaves a station at 10:50 pm and reaches the next station, 135 km away, at 12:20 am. What is its average speed?
questions.a: The journey takes 1 h 30 min = 1.5 h, so the speed is 135 / 1.5 = 90 km/h. Treating 1 h 30 min as 1.30 h gives 103.8 km/h; subtracting 10.50 from 12.20 as decimals gives 1.70 and 79.4 km/h; 135 km/h forgets to divide by the time.

questions.q: Raju cycles to school along a short lane, 2.4 km in 12 minutes, and returns by a longer lane, 3 km in 20 minutes. (a) Find his speed to school in km/h. (b) Find his speed on the way back in km/h. (c) Which trip is faster, and by how much? (d) Find his average speed for the whole round trip. (e) Raju says the average speed is the mean of the two speeds. Show that he is wrong.
questions.a: (a) 2.4 km in 0.2 h = 12 km/h. (b) 3 km in 1/3 h = 9 km/h. (c) The trip to school is faster by 3 km/h. (d) Total 5.4 km in 32 min = 5.4 / (32/60) = 10.125 km/h. (e) The mean of 12 and 9 is 10.5 km/h, which is not 10.125 km/h, because he spent more time at the slower speed.
s: Part (a): 12 km/h
Part (b): 9 km/h
Part (c): to school, faster by 3 km/h
Part (d): 5.4 km in 32 min, average 10.125 km/h
Part (e): the mean 10.5 km/h differs because more time was spent at the slower speed

questions.q: Tanvi leaves home at 8:10 am for a market 1.8 km away and walks at 1.5 m/s. Her brother leaves home 10 minutes later and cycles the same road at 4 m/s. Who reaches the market first, and by how much?
questions.a: Tanvi needs 1800 / 1.5 = 1200 s = 20 min and arrives at 8:30; her brother needs 1800 / 4 = 450 s = 7.5 min and arrives at 8:27:30, so he is first by 2 min 30 s. Forgetting his 10-minute later start gives 12 min 30 s; ignoring speeds and going by the earlier start gives Tanvi.

questions.q: A scooter travels at 36 km/h on a straight road. (a) Express its speed in m/s. (b) A rider takes 2.5 s to react after seeing an obstacle. How far does the scooter travel in that time?
questions.a: (a) 36 x 1000 / 3600 = 10 m/s. (b) Distance = speed x time = 10 x 2.5 = 25 m.
s: Part (a): 10 m/s
Part (b): 25 m

questions.q: A cyclist rides at 18 km/h, a runner at 6 m/s, a bus at 0.5 km per minute and a horse at 15 m/s. (a) Express each speed in m/s. (b) Arrange them from slowest to fastest. (c) Find the time each takes to cover 600 m. (d) By how many seconds does the fastest beat the slowest over 600 m? (e) Give a reason for converting all speeds to one unit before comparing.
questions.a: (a) Cyclist 5 m/s, runner 6 m/s, bus about 8.33 m/s, horse 15 m/s. (b) Cyclist, runner, bus, horse. (c) 120 s, 100 s, 72 s and 40 s. (d) 120 - 40 = 80 s. (e) Speeds in different units, such as km/h and m/s, cannot be compared by looking at the numbers.
s: Part (a): 5, 6, 8.33 and 15 m/s
Part (b): cyclist, runner, bus, horse
Part (c): 120 s, 100 s, 72 s and 40 s
Part (d): 80 s
Part (e): numbers in different units cannot be compared directly

questions.q: A cyclist covers 30 km in 2 hours but only 10 km in the first hour. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: Average speed is total distance divided by total time, 30 / 2 = 15 km/h; since 10 km was covered in the first hour, 30 - 10 = 20 km was covered in the second. Her speed was not constant, so 15 km/h is not her speed at every instant.
o: Her average speed is 15 km/h and she covered 20 km in the second hour
Her speed was 15 km/h at every instant of the ride
Her average speed is 10 km/h, because the first hour decides it
Her average speed is 20 km/h, because the second hour decides it

questions.q:
On Sports Day three teams each ran a different race length on a straight track. Team Red ran 400 m in 80 s, Team Blue ran 300 m in 50 s and Team Green ran 200 m in 36 s. The school can send only one team to a 600 m relay at the district event, and the coach wants the team that would finish it first.
(a) Find the speed of each team in m/s (two decimal places).
(b) How long would each team take to cover 600 m at its speed?
(c) By how many seconds does the quickest team beat the next one?
(d) Blue is expected to slow down by 5% over the longer race. Does it still beat Green? Decide which team to send.
questions.a: (a) Red 5.00 m/s, Blue 6.00 m/s, Green 5.56 m/s. (b) Red 120 s, Blue 100 s, Green 108 s. (c) Blue beats Green by 8 s. (d) Blue at 5% slower is 5.7 m/s and takes 600 / 5.7 = about 105.3 s, still under Green's 108 s, so send Blue.
s: Part (b): 120 s, 100 s and 108 s
Part (c): Blue beats Green by 8 s
Part (d): Blue at 5.7 m/s takes about 105.3 s, still ahead of Green, so send Blue

questions.q:
Statement I: A speed of 54 km/h is greater than a speed of 15 m/s.
Statement II: A train moving at 90 km/h takes 4 h to cover 360 km.
Statement III: A cyclist covering 18 km in 1.5 h has the same speed as another covering 20 km in 1.5 h.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Only II is correct. I is false: 15 m/s = 54 km/h, so the speeds are equal. III is false: 18 / 1.5 = 12 km/h but 20 / 1.5 = 13.3 km/h.

questions.q: Sunil says, "Speed is the distance covered in one second, so it can only be written in metres per second." Check his claim.
questions.a: Partly right. Speed is the distance covered in a unit time, and the SI unit, metre per second, uses one second. But the unit time may also be a minute or an hour, so speed can be written in other units such as km/h.
s: Gives the verdict partly right
Accepts that m/s is the SI unit of speed
Corrects 'only': the unit time may be a minute or an hour, giving units such as km/h

questions.q: Priya says she cycled 15 km in 30 minutes, so her speed was 50 km/h. Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: 15 km / 0.5 h = 30 km/h. At 50 km/h she would cover 25 km in 30 min, not 15.
s: 30 minutes = 0.5 h
Speed = 15 / 0.5 = 30 km/h
30 km/h is not 50 km/h; at 50 km/h she would cover 25 km in 30 min

questions.q: On a 400 m track athlete P runs 4 laps in 6 minutes and athlete Q runs 5 laps in 8 minutes 20 seconds. (a) Find the speed of each in m/s (two decimal places). (b) If they keep these speeds for 10 minutes, how many metres is P ahead of Q?
questions.a: (a) P: 1600 m in 360 s = 4.44 m/s; Q: 2000 m in 500 s = 4.00 m/s. (b) In 600 s P runs 2666.7 m and Q 2400 m, so P is ahead by about 266.7 m.
s: Part (a): 4.44 m/s and 4.00 m/s
Part (b): about 266.7 m

questions.q: Make up a short situation in which two travellers go different distances in different times but have exactly the same speed. Show the working that proves the speeds are equal.
questions.a: Example: a bus covers 120 km in 2 h, so its speed is 120 / 2 = 60 km/h; a car covers 45 km in 0.75 h (45 minutes), so its speed is 45 / 0.75 = 60 km/h. The distances and times differ but the speeds are equal.
s: A situation with two different distances and two different times
Working that gives the first speed
Working that gives the same value for the second speed

questions.q: A cyclist rides at 18 km/h for 40 minutes. (a) How far does she go? (b) How long would she take for the same distance at 24 km/h?
s: Part (a): 12 km
Part (b): 30 minutes

questions.q: A bus averages 40 km/h. It leaves a town at 7:45 am and reaches the next town at 10:15 am. How far apart are the towns?
questions.a: Time = 10:15 - 7:45 = 2.5 h, so distance = 40 x 2.5 = 100 km. Reading the time as 2.70 h gives 108 km; dividing gives 16 km; adding gives 42.5 km.

questions.q:
Between Station P and Station Q, 108 km apart, three trains run. The passenger train takes 3 h, the express takes 1.5 h and the superfast takes 1.2 h. Fares are ₹60, ₹120 and ₹180 respectively. Mr Rao leaves Station P at 8:00 am and must reach Station Q by 9:45 am. He wants the cheapest train that gets him there in time.
(a) Find the speed of each train in km/h.
(b) Express the express train's speed in m/s.
(c) At the superfast's speed, how long would it need for 270 km?
(d) Which train should Mr Rao take? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) 36, 72, 90 km/h. (b) 20 m/s. (c) 3 h. (d) Express: arrives 9:30 am for ₹120; superfast also in time but costs ₹180; passenger is late.
s: Part (a): 36, 72 and 90 km/h
Part (d): express; it arrives at 9:30 am and is cheaper than the superfast; the passenger train arrives at 11:00 am

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A speed of 5 m/s is greater than a speed of 17 km/h.
Reason (R): A body moving at 5 m/s covers 5 x 3600 m in an hour, which is 18 km.
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: converting 5 m/s to 18 km/h in the same unit shows it exceeds 17 km/h.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
Column I
1. 36 km/h
2. 90 km/h
3. 72 km/h
4. 18 km/h
Column II
a. 25 m/s
b. 5 m/s
c. 20 m/s
d. 10 m/s
questions.a: 36 km/h = 10 m/s (d); 90 km/h = 25 m/s (a); 72 km/h = 20 m/s (c); 18 km/h = 5 m/s (b); each is the km/h figure divided by 3.6.

questions.q: Rahul writes: "A car covers 150 m in 10 s, so its speed is 15 km/h." (a) Find his mistake. (b) Give the speed correctly in km/h.
questions.a: (a) 150 / 10 = 15 is in metres per second, not km/h, because the distance is in metres and the time in seconds. (b) 15 m/s = 15 x 3.6 = 54 km/h.
s: Part (a): 15 is in m/s because distance is in metres and time in seconds
Part (b): 54 km/h

questions.q: A train runs at 72 km/h for 25 minutes. A cheetah runs at 30 m/s for 7 minutes. Which covers the greater distance, and by how much?
questions.a: The train covers 72 x 25/60 = 30 km and the cheetah 30 x 420 = 12,600 m = 12.6 km, so the train covers 17.4 km more. Comparing the numbers 72 and 30, or 25 and 7, without converting units gives the wrong ranking.

questions.q: True or False: Runner P covers 200 m in 30 s and runner Q covers 150 m in 21 s. Since P ran farther, P has the higher speed.
questions.a: False. P's speed is 200 / 30 = 6.67 m/s and Q's is 150 / 21 = 7.14 m/s, so Q is faster; the distance alone does not decide speed, distance and time together do.
s: Verdict: False
Reason or correction that rests on the chapter

questions.q: Between two stations 48 km apart the passenger train takes 1 h 20 min and the express takes 50 min. (a) Find the speed of each in km/h. (b) How many minutes does the express save?
questions.a: (a) Passenger: 48 / (4/3) = 36 km/h; express: 48 / (5/6) = 57.6 km/h. (b) 80 - 50 = 30 minutes.
s: Part (a): 36 km/h and 57.6 km/h
Part (b): 30 minutes

questions.q: A taxi's odometer reads 5,420 km when the meter starts at 9:15 am and 5,452 km when the trip ends at 10:00 am. The driver says the speedometer once showed 80 km/h. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: The distance is 5,452 - 5,420 = 32 km in 45 min = 0.75 h, so the average speed is 32 / 0.75 = about 42.7 km/h; an instantaneous reading of 80 km/h does not decide the average. Treating 45 min as 0.45 h gives 71.1 km/h; 32 km/h forgets to divide by the time.
o: The average speed is about 42.7 km/h; 80 km/h was the speed at one instant
The average speed is 80 km/h, because it is the highest speed the speedometer showed
The average speed is about 71.1 km/h, found by dividing 32 km by 0.45 h
The average speed is 32 km/h, because the distance covered is 32 km

questions.q: True or False: On a straight highway a car's speedometer reads 60 km/h at every moment for 3 minutes, although the car crawled through a town just before and after. During those 3 minutes the car is in uniform linear motion.
questions.a: True. The speed is constant along a straight line for those 3 minutes, so the car covers equal distances (1 km each minute, 3 km in all) in equal intervals; the slow motion in the town does not matter, because uniform motion is judged for the stretch considered.
s: Gives the verdict True
Reason: constant speed on a straight line gives equal distances in equal intervals, 1 km every minute

questions.q: Train M covers 30 km in each of the four 15-minute intervals between 10:00 and 11:00. Train N covers 20, 40, 25 and 35 km in the same four intervals. Sunita says, "Both are in uniform motion, since both cover 120 km in the hour." Check her claim.
questions.a: Wrong. Equal averages (120 km/h) do not make motion uniform; N covers 20, 40, 25 and 35 km in equal intervals, so it is non-uniform, while M is uniform.
s: Verdict: wrong
Both cover 120 km in 1 h, so both have an average speed of 120 km/h
N covers unequal distances in equal intervals, so only M is uniform

questions.q: A scooter on a straight road is at 0, 10, 20, 30, 45 and 60 m at successive 5 s intervals. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: The distances covered in the five 5 s intervals are 10, 10, 10, 15 and 15 m: equal for the first 15 s (uniform), but not equal over the whole 25 s, so the whole motion is non-uniform.
o: Uniform for the first 15 s, non-uniform over the whole 25 s
Uniform for the whole 25 s, since the scooter never stops
Non-uniform even in the first 15 s, since the position keeps changing
Uniform for the whole 25 s, since an average speed of 2.4 m/s exists

questions.q: An object moves along a straight line. Which single observation is enough to show that its motion is non-uniform?
questions.a: Uniform motion needs equal distances in equal intervals; 12 m and then 15 m in equal one-second intervals breaks this, so the motion is non-uniform. Equal distances in equal times are what uniform motion looks like, and a total distance or an average speed says nothing about equal intervals.
o: It covers 12 m in one second and 15 m in the next second
It covers 50 m in the first 10 s and 50 m in the next 10 s
Its average speed over the whole journey is 40 km/h

questions.q:
Neha's father starts a car journey at 8:00 am when the odometer reads 24,560 km. At 10:30 am it reads 24,710 km. During the drive Neha notes the speedometer reading 60 km/h on the highway, 20 km/h in a town and 0 at a railway gate. They must reach her grandmother's house, 90 km further, by 1:00 pm. The route through the next town has 30 km at 20 km/h, then 60 km of highway at 60 km/h, and the railway gate usually delays vehicles by 10 minutes. A bypass is 110 km long and can be driven at 55 km/h all the way.
(a) How far has the car gone by 10:30 am, and what is its average speed so far?
(b) Is the motion uniform? Justify using the speedometer readings.
(c) Find the time needed to reach the house by the town route (with the gate delay) and by the bypass.
(d) Which route should they take, and why would the earlier average speed have misled them?
questions.a: (a) 24,710 - 24,560 = 150 km; 150 / 2.5 h = 60 km/h. (b) Non-uniform: the speedometer showed 60, 20 and 0 km/h, so the speed changed. (c) Town route: 30/20 = 1.5 h, 60/60 = 1 h and 10 min, a total of 2 h 40 min, arriving at 1:10 pm. Bypass: 110 / 55 = 2 h, arriving at 12:30 pm. (d) Take the bypass: it arrives at 12:30 pm, before 1:00 pm, whereas the town route arrives at 1:10 pm. The average of 60 km/h suggested 90 / 60 = 1.5 h and a noon arrival, but the town stretch at 20 km/h and the gate delay lower the average.
s: Part (a): 150 km and 60 km/h
Part (b): non-uniform, because the speedometer readings 60, 20 and 0 km/h show a changing speed
Part (c): town route 2 h 40 min (1:10 pm), bypass 2 h (12:30 pm)
Part (d): bypass, because it arrives before 1:00 pm, while the earlier average speed hid the slow town stretch and the gate delay

questions.q:
During a cross-country run on a straight road, the coach records Varun's distance in each 2-minute interval: 500 m, 500 m, 500 m, 600 m and 400 m. She says, "His average speed is 15 km/h, so he ran steadily throughout."
(a) For which intervals was his motion uniform, and at what speed in m/min?
(b) Find his total distance and average speed in km/h.
(c) Is the whole run uniform? Give the evidence.
(d) Evaluate the coach's statement.
questions.a: (a) First three intervals, 250 m/min. (b) 2500 m, 15 km/h. (c) No, distances 600 m and 400 m are unequal. (d) Average speed 15 km/h is correct, but the run was not steady.
s: Part (a): first three intervals, 500 / 2 = 250 m/min
Part (b): 2500 m in 10 min = 2.5 km in 1/6 h = 15 km/h
Part (c): no; 600 m and 400 m differ from 500 m in equal intervals
Part (d): the average is right but 'steadily' is wrong, since the speed changed

questions.q: At 8:10 am the speedometer of a car reads 50 km/h, and at 8:40 am it again reads 50 km/h. Anita says the car moved in uniform linear motion between the two readings. What is the correct response?
questions.a: A speedometer shows the speed only at the instant of the reading. The car might have slowed down and speeded up between 8:10 and 8:40, so the readings alone do not show equal distances in equal intervals. The 25 km is only the distance that would be covered if the speed had stayed constant.
o: Not proven: the speed may have changed in between
Correct: equal readings show a constant speed throughout
Correct: the car covered 25 km in the half hour, so its motion is uniform
Not proven: a speedometer cannot show the speed of a car

questions.q: An object moving on a straight line is found at 0, 12, 24, 40 and 52 m at 0, 5, 10, 15 and 20 s. In which interval does its motion differ from the rest?
questions.a: The distances in the four 5 s intervals are 12, 12, 16 and 12 m; the interval from 10 s to 15 s breaks the pattern of equal distances in equal times.

questions.q: A cyclist covers 12 km at 24 km/h and then another 12 km at 12 km/h. Her average speed for the 24 km is ___ km/h.

A bus covers 8 km in each of the first three 10-minute intervals, stands still during the fourth 10-minute interval and covers 8 km in the fifth. (a) Is its motion uniform over the 50 minutes? Give a reason. (b) Find its average speed over the 50 minutes in km/h.
questions.a: (a) No, because it covers 8 km in some equal intervals and nothing in the fourth, so the distances are unequal. (b) Total 32 km in 50 min = 32 / (5/6) = 38.4 km/h.
s: Part (a): not uniform because the fourth interval has no distance
Part (b): 32 km in 50 minutes, 38.4 km/h

questions.q: A student says that an object in uniform linear motion covered 30 m in the first 10 s and 80 m in the first 20 s. Show that this cannot be true.
questions.a: In uniform motion equal distances are covered in equal intervals. 30 m in the first 10 s means 30 m in the next 10 s too, so 60 m in 20 s, not 80 m. The distance in the second 10 s would be 80 - 30 = 50 m, which is not equal to 30 m.
s: States that uniform motion needs equal distances in equal intervals
Works out that 30 m in each 10 s gives 60 m in 20 s
Concludes that 80 m in 20 s contradicts this (the second 10 s would need 50 m)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A bus that covers 6 km in every 10 minutes along a straight road for an hour is in uniform linear motion.
Reason (R): The bus covers a total of 36 km in that hour.
questions.a: Both true, but R does not explain A; the reason is that the bus covers equal distances (6 km) in equal intervals.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: (a) Why does the chapter use average speed when it speaks of the speed of a journey? (b) A coach covers 180 km in 4 h including its halts. What is its average speed?
questions.a: (a) Uniform linear motion is an idealisation; objects seldom keep a constant speed over long distances or long intervals, so average speed is used. (b) 180 / 4 = 45 km/h.
s: Part (a): objects seldom move at constant speed over long distances or times, so average speed is used
Part (b): 45 km/h

questions.q:
Statement I: A car whose speedometer reads 60 km/h throughout a straight 5-minute stretch covers 5 km and is in uniform linear motion over those minutes.
Statement II: A scooter that covers 500 m in the first minute, stands still in the second minute and covers 500 m in the third minute has non-uniform motion over the three minutes.
Statement III: The same scooter's average speed over the three minutes is about 5.6 m/s.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three are correct. I: 60 km/h for 5 minutes covers 60 x 5/60 = 5 km at a constant speed. II: the distances in equal intervals are 500 m, 0 and 500 m. III: 1000 m / 180 s = about 5.6 m/s.

questions.q: A driver plans a 120 km trip. He drives the first 60 km at 60 km/h and says, "To average 80 km/h for the whole trip I only need to do the second half at 100 km/h." (a) How long does the first half take? (b) What total time gives an average of 80 km/h for 120 km? (c) How much time is then left for the second half? (d) At what speed must he drive the second half? (e) What average speed does he actually get if he drives it at 100 km/h?
questions.a: (a) 60 / 60 = 1 h. (b) 120 / 80 = 1.5 h. (c) 1.5 - 1 = 0.5 h. (d) 60 / 0.5 = 120 km/h, so his plan is wrong. (e) The second half takes 60 / 100 = 0.6 h, so the total is 1.6 h and the average is 120 / 1.6 = 75 km/h.
s: Part (a): 1 h
Part (b): 1.5 h
Part (c): 0.5 h
Part (d): 120 km/h, so 100 km/h is not enough
Part (e): 75 km/h

questions.q: A car's odometer reads 8,420 km at 6:00 am and 8,500 km at 7:30 am. It stood at a level crossing for 10 minutes. (a) Find its average speed for the whole 90 minutes in km/h. (b) Find its average speed while it was actually moving.
questions.a: (a) 80 km in 1.5 h = 53.3 km/h. (b) The moving time is 90 - 10 = 80 min = 4/3 h, so 80 / (4/3) = 60 km/h.
s: Part (a): about 53.3 km/h
Part (b): 60 km/h for the moving time of 80 minutes

questions.q: Car P covers 15 m in every 5 s for 25 s. Car Q covers 10 m, 20 m, 15 m, 20 m and 10 m in successive 5 s intervals. Compare their motion: (a) type of P, (b) type of Q, (c) average speeds, (d) what the equal averages show, (e) which type is more common in daily life.
questions.a: P is uniform; Q is non-uniform. Both cover 75 m in 25 s, an average of 3 m/s, so equal averages can hide different motion. Non-uniform motion is more common in everyday life.
s: Part (a): P is uniform, equal distances in equal intervals
Part (b): Q is non-uniform, unequal distances
Part (c): both 75 m in 25 s = 3 m/s
Part (d): equal average speed does not mean same type of motion
Part (e): non-uniform is more common; uniform motion is an idealisation

questions.q: Make up a scooter journey in four successive 5-minute intervals, giving the distance covered in each interval, so that the motion is uniform in the first three intervals but non-uniform over the whole twenty minutes. Give the average speed in km/h.
questions.a: Example: 2 km, 2 km, 2 km and 3 km. The first three intervals have equal distances (uniform) but the fourth differs, so the whole motion is non-uniform. Total 9 km in 20 minutes = 9 / (1/3) = 27 km/h.
s: Three equal distances followed by a different fourth distance
Says the first three intervals are uniform and the whole journey is not
Average speed worked out correctly (27 km/h for the example)

questions.q: An object covers 4 m, 4 m, 4 m, 6 m and 8 m in five successive 2-second intervals. (a) For how many seconds is its motion uniform, and at what speed? (b) What is its average speed over the 10 seconds?
questions.a: (a) It is uniform for the first 6 s (three equal distances of 4 m), at 4/2 = 2 m/s. (b) Total 26 m in 10 s = 2.6 m/s.
s: Part (a): 6 s at 2 m/s
Part (b): 26 m in 10 s, 2.6 m/s
